title: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And contrary to what has always been assumed, I suspect that this is actually how the apparent randomness that one sometimes sees in shapes formed by crystalline materials often comes about.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “The Growth of Crystals” (from p. 369), p. 373. Scope: growth shapes of crystals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Crystal shapes can be quantified, but assigning randomness to intrinsic dynamics requires unusually complete initial-condition and environmental measurements. Existing public records permit only selected case studies. Even close deterministic fits may not discriminate chaos from amplified unobserved noise.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use repeated crystal-growth trajectories with measured seed and environmental perturbations to fit deterministic instability and exogenous-noise models, then compare held-out path distributions and repeatability. Intrinsic generation is supported only if deterministic dynamics explain residual variation better than measured external fluctuations across crystal types.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Model non-identifiability limits causal attribution.

Often spans an undefined population of crystalline materials.

Unmeasured microscopic seed defects can masquerade as intrinsic randomness.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.28
discriminating power: 0.38
analysis feasibility: 0.48
data existence: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The discriminating observation is run-to-run repeatability under fixed conditions, not a simulation that looks rough. That observation exists for a few crystalline systems and is missing for most materials, so often across crystal shapes cannot be read off current public collections. The claim is testable on a restricted scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Repeat crystal-growth runs from simple seeds in a controlled environment and compare the irregular outline across runs. Outlines that recur in detail would favor intrinsic generation by the growth rule; outlines that change with run, seed noise, or uncontrolled environment would favor external randomness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A deterministic model that looks irregular does not show that real crystals use that mechanism.

Repeat-run shape archives are rare outside a few laboratory systems such as ice and electrodeposits.

data existence: 0.4
